CHAPTER 2.2 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.2 · LEARNING AREA 2 · JANUARY

Decimals and percentages

3.47 m in the long jump, 9.58 s for 100 m, €1.29 for a bread roll, 25% off: numbers with a decimal point and the per cent sign are everywhere. In this chapter you learn what the places after the decimal point mean, how to turn decimal fractions into decimals and back again, how to compare and round decimals, and what per cent means.

9 LESSONS3 UNITS1 LOOK AHEAD
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • extend the place value table by tenths, hundredths and thousandths
  • write decimal fractions as decimals and the other way round, also for quantities
  • compare, order and round decimals
  • know how to write percentages for 1%, 10%, 20%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100%

1 m = 100 cm

1 kg = 1,000 g

$\tfrac44 = 1$

$100 \div 4 = 25$ cents

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Decimal fractions and decimals

In the long jump the display shows 3.47 m. That is 3 m and 47 cm. A centimetre is a hundredth of a metre, so 3.47 m is the same as $3\text{ m} + \tfrac{47}{100}\text{ m}$.

Fractions with the denominator 10, 100, 1,000, … are called decimal fractions. You can write them without a fraction line, with a decimal point. For this the place value table continues to the right: after the ones comes the decimal point, then the tenths, the hundredths and the thousandths. Each place is again worth ten times as much as the one to its right.

Numbers with a decimal point are called decimals. Zeros at the end after the decimal point do not change the value: $0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500$, because five tenths are fifty hundredths.

KEY POINT · DECIMALS
ThHTOthth
3.047

t tenths $\left(\tfrac{1}{10}\right)$, h hundredths $\left(\tfrac{1}{100}\right)$, th thousandths $\left(\tfrac{1}{1{,}000}\right)$: $3.047 = 3 + \tfrac{47}{1{,}000}$

Decimal fraction → decimal: as many places after the decimal point as the denominator has zeros: $\tfrac{7}{10} = 0.7$, $\tfrac{23}{100} = 0.23$, $\tfrac{9}{1{,}000} = 0.009$.

Decimal → decimal fraction: count the places after the decimal point: $0.045 = \tfrac{45}{1{,}000}$.

Quantities: 1 cm is a hundredth of a metre, 1 g a thousandth of a kilogram, 1 cent a hundredth of a euro.

Reading it correctly: 3.47 is read “three point four seven”, not “three point forty-seven”.

INTERACTIVE · THE EXTENDED PLACE VALUE TABLE

Change the digits before and after the decimal point. On the right you see the number as a decimal and as a decimal fraction.

EXAMPLE 1 · SIX, BUT WHERE?

Write as a decimal fraction and as a decimal: six tenths, six hundredths, six thousandths.

Each time the 6 moves one place further to the right; zeros fill the gaps.

$\tfrac{6}{10} = 0.6$; $\tfrac{6}{100} = 0.06$; $\tfrac{6}{1{,}000} = 0.006$

EXAMPLE 2 · QUANTITIES WITH A DECIMAL POINT

Write with a decimal point: a) 2 m 35 cm in m   b) 4 euros 3 cents in €   c) 1 kg 20 g in kg

a) 35 cm are 35 hundredths of a metre. b) 3 cents are 3 hundredths of a euro. c) 20 g are 20 thousandths of a kilogram.

a) 2.35 m   b) €4.03   c) 1.020 kg = 1.02 kg

EXERCISES

Write as a decimal: a) $\tfrac{7}{10}$   b) $\tfrac{23}{100}$   c) $\tfrac{9}{1{,}000}$   d) $3 + \tfrac{41}{100}$

a) 0.7   b) 0.23   c) 0.009   d) 3.41

Write as a decimal fraction: a) 0.9   b) 0.37   c) 0.205   d) 0.04

a) $\tfrac{9}{10}$   b) $\tfrac{37}{100}$   c) $\tfrac{205}{1{,}000}$   d) $\tfrac{4}{100}$

Write with a decimal point in the larger unit: a) 5 m 7 cm in m   b) 12 euros 50 cents in €   c) 2 kg 300 g in kg   d) 750 g in kg

a) 5.07 m   b) €12.50   c) 2.3 kg   d) 0.75 kg

What is the value of the digit 4? a) 0.4   b) 2.04   c) 13.004   d) 40.1

a) 4 tenths   b) 4 hundredths   c) 4 thousandths   d) 4 tens

Jonas says: “0.25 is bigger than 0.3, because 25 is bigger than 3.” Use the place value table to explain his mistake.

You must not read the digits after the decimal point like a natural number. 0.25 has 2 tenths and 5 hundredths, 0.3 has 3 tenths. If you write $0.3 = 0.30$, you can see: 30 hundredths are more than 25 hundredths. So $0.3 > 0.25$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Write $\tfrac{7}{100}$ as a decimal.

7 hundredths: 0.07

Write 0.125 as a decimal fraction. What is the denominator?

Three places after the decimal point: $\tfrac{125}{1{,}000}$

Write 2 m 5 cm in metres.

5 cm are 5 hundredths of a metre: 2.05 m.

UNIT 23 LESSONS

2Comparing, ordering and rounding

In the class 100 m race Lea ran 15.8 s, Ben 15.75 s and Mia 15.09 s. Who was the fastest? The wholes are the same. In the tenths Mia has a 0, Ben a 7 and Lea an 8. Mia was the fastest, Lea the slowest.

You compare decimals like natural numbers, from left to right: first the wholes, then the tenths, then the hundredths. So that both numbers have the same number of places, you can add zeros at the end: $15.8 = 15.80$.

Rounding works as for natural numbers: the digit to the right of the rounding place decides. How exactly you round depends on the situation: amounts of money to the nearest cent, that is two places, people’s heights to the nearest centimetre.

KEY POINT · COMPARING AND ROUNDING

Comparing: from the left, place by place. Fill missing places with zeros: $0.7 = 0.70 > 0.65$.

Rounding: 0 to 4 round down, 5 to 9 round up. $3.476 \approx 3.48$ (to hundredths) $\approx 3.5$ (to tenths) $\approx 3$ (to whole numbers).

More digits does not mean bigger: $0.7 > 0.699$.

Keep the zero at the end: $2.96 \approx 3.0$ to tenths. The zero shows how exactly the number was rounded.

INTERACTIVE · ROUNDING UNDER THE MAGNIFYING GLASS

Choose the rounding place. The section always goes from one possible result to the other.

EXAMPLE 3 · ORDERING

Put in order from smallest to biggest: 0.5; 0.45; 0.405; 0.54.

With three places: 0.500; 0.450; 0.405; 0.540. Now you compare them like natural numbers: 405, 450, 500, 540.

$0.405 < 0.45 < 0.5 < 0.54$

EXAMPLE 4 · AT THE PETROL STATION

A litre of petrol costs €1.769. How much is that rounded to the nearest cent?

Cents are hundredths of a euro. To the right of the hundredths place is a 9: round up.

$\text{€}1.769 \approx \text{€}1.77$

EXERCISES

Put in $<$, $>$ or $=$: a) $2.7 \;☐\; 2.07$   b) $0.5 \;☐\; 0.50$   c) $3.099 \;☐\; 3.1$   d) $12.4 \;☐\; 12.39$

a) $>$   b) $=$   c) $<$   d) $>$

Round to tenths and to hundredths: a) 4.736   b) 0.982   c) 12.045   d) 7.995

a) 4.7 and 4.74   b) 1.0 and 0.98   c) 12.0 and 12.05   d) 8.0 and 8.00

Put in order from smallest to biggest: 1.1; 1.01; 1.11; 1.101; 1.011

$1.01 < 1.011 < 1.1 < 1.101 < 1.11$

Long jump in class 5b: Ben 3.45 m, Lia 3.5 m, Can 3.4 m, Ida 3.54 m. Who comes in which place?

With two places: 3.45; 3.50; 3.40; 3.54. 1st place Ida, 2nd place Lia, 3rd place Ben, 4th place Can.

Find three decimals between 0.3 and 0.31. Is there also one between 0.301 and 0.302?

Add zeros: 0.300 and 0.310. What lies in between?

For example 0.301; 0.305 and 0.309. Between 0.301 and 0.302 lies, for example, 0.3015: with one more place you can always find a number in between.

TEST YOURSELF!

Round 5.849 to tenths.

To the right of the 8 is a 4: round down, 5.8.

Round 0.996 to hundredths.

To the right of the second 9 is a 6: round up. 0.99 becomes 1.00.

Which number is the biggest: 0.8; 0.79; 0.815; 0.08?

With three places: 0.800; 0.790; 0.815; 0.080. The biggest is 0.815.

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Per cent

In the shop it says: “25% off”. The sign % is called per cent, which means “out of a hundred”. 25% is 25 out of 100, so $\tfrac{25}{100} = 0.25$. That is a quarter.

Per cent is a third way of writing parts of a whole, alongside fractions and decimals. You can see it well on a hundred square: one square out of 100 is 1%, ten squares are 10%, half is 50%, all the squares are 100%, that is the whole.

You can calculate with simple percentages if you think of the matching fraction: 50% of €30 is half, so €15. 10% of €80 is a tenth, so €8.

KEY POINT · PER CENT
Percentage1%10%20%25%50%75%100%
Fraction$\tfrac{1}{100}$$\tfrac{1}{10}$$\tfrac15$$\tfrac14$$\tfrac12$$\tfrac34$1
Decimal0.010.10.20.250.50.751

Per cent means “out of a hundred”: $25\% = \tfrac{25}{100}$. 100% is the whole.

How to write it: in English the per cent sign comes straight after the number, without a space: 25%.

Over 100%: that happens when something becomes more than the whole, for example 200% for twice the amount.

INTERACTIVE · THE HUNDRED SQUARE

Set the numerator; the denominator stays 100. On the right you see the fraction as a decimal and as a percentage.

EXAMPLE 5 · THREE WAYS OF WRITING IT

On a hundred square, 30 squares are coloured. Give the fraction in three ways.

30 out of 100: $\tfrac{30}{100}$. That is 3 tenths.

$\tfrac{30}{100} = \tfrac{3}{10} = 0.3 = 30\%$

EXAMPLE 6 · DISCOUNT

A jacket costs €80. In the sale there is 25% off. How much do you save, and what does the jacket cost then?

25% is a quarter: $\text{€}80 \div 4 = \text{€}20$.

You save €20, and the jacket costs €60.

EXERCISES

Write as a percentage: a) 0.5   b) $\tfrac14$   c) 0.1   d) $\tfrac34$   e) 1

a) 50%   b) 25%   c) 10%   d) 75%   e) 100%

Write as a fraction and as a decimal: a) 20%   b) 1%   c) 75%

a) $\tfrac15 = 0.2$   b) $\tfrac{1}{100} = 0.01$   c) $\tfrac34 = 0.75$

Work out: a) 50% of €46   b) 10% of 250 m   c) 25% of 120 pupils   d) 1% of €3,000

a) €23   b) 25 m   c) $120 \div 4 = 30$   d) $3{,}000 \div 100 = 30$, so €30

In a survey of 100 people, 20 say “yes” and 25 say “no”. The others do not know. Give all three shares as percentages.

Yes 20%, no 25%, don’t know $100 - 20 - 25 = 55$, so 55%. Together 100%.

Which offer is cheaper? Shop A: 25% off €60. Shop B: €10 off €55.

A: 25% of €60 is €15, so you pay €45. B: $55 - 10 = 45$, so €45. Both offers cost exactly the same.

TEST YOURSELF!

What percentage is a quarter?

$\tfrac14 = \tfrac{25}{100} = 25\%$

Write 20% as a decimal.

$\tfrac{20}{100} = 0.20 = 0.2$

How much is 75% of €40?

A quarter of €40 is €10, so three quarters are €30.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Three ways of writing it: Write as a fraction, as a decimal and as a percentage: half, one tenth, three quarters.

$\tfrac12 = 0.5 = 50\%$   $\tfrac{1}{10} = 0.1 = 10\%$   $\tfrac34 = 0.75 = 75\%$

Mixed ordering: Put in order from smallest to biggest: 0.3; $\tfrac14$; 35%; 0.05; $\tfrac12$

As decimals: 0.3; 0.25; 0.35; 0.05; 0.5. So $0.05 < \tfrac14 < 0.3 < 35\% < \tfrac12$.

Rounded too roughly: In the 50 m run Tim ran 8.24 s, Lars 8.2 s and Ole 8.42 s. Who came first? Then round each time to tenths. What do you notice?

Lars with 8.20 s, ahead of Tim with 8.24 s and Ole with 8.42 s. Rounded to tenths, Lars and Tim both have 8.2 s. For a ranking you have to measure more precisely.

Battery: A tablet shows 40% battery. Fully charged, the battery lasts 10 hours. About how long will the rest last?

$40\% = \tfrac{4}{10}$. One tenth of 10 hours is 1 hour, four tenths are 4 hours.

EXCURSIONSPORT

Hundredths of a second

On 16 August 2009 the Jamaican Usain Bolt ran the 100 m at the World Championships in Berlin in 9.58 seconds. That is still the world record today. In a race like this the time is measured electronically, to the nearest hundredth of a second. The starting gun sets the clock going, a camera at the finish stops it.

In the past, judges stopped the time by hand. Because a person cannot press a button that quickly, these times were only given in tenths of a second. Since 1 January 1977 the world federation has required fully automatic timing to hundredths for sprint records. In 1968 Jim Hines ran 9.95 s at the Olympic Games in Mexico City. That was the first electronically timed world record under 10 seconds.

Try it yourself: By how many hundredths of a second was Bolt faster than Hines? Round both times to tenths. Can you still see the difference then?

9.95 s are 995 hundredths, 9.58 s are 958 hundredths. Bolt was 37 hundredths of a second faster. Rounded to tenths: 10.0 s and 9.6 s; the difference can still be seen clearly.

Sources: World Athletics, world record list, men’s 100 m (worldathletics.org/records). On timing: rule of the world federation IAAF, in force since 1 January 1977; overview “Men’s 100 metres world record progression”, Wikipedia (English).
